When talking "longevity", what do you mean?

The reason I ask is because there are a larger number of 100 year old wood windows (I have a house with 26 of them myself). So long as they're kept painted, they will last pretty much forever. Vinyl, not so much. Go with the cheapest of the cheap vinyl and you'll be replacing them in about 10 years. Go for the best quality vinyl windows and you'll probably get 40~50 years. But there's a problem, that's just talking about the Frame, if you buy double/triple pane glass, Those will fail (normally they get cloudy/opaque) at some point and need to be replaced. The oldest of those I've seen are usually less than 30 years old.

FWIW, my wood windows are in a highly humid climate that ranges in temp about like you, lots of rain. Even completely neglected with no paint remaining, they were not rotted/damaged beyond sun fading. A light sanding removed that and allowed me to paint them again. The way you get insulation with Single-pane windows is through storm windows where you effectively separate the two panes.

But, if I were going to buy units of double-pane windows, I'd probably opt for all wood or wood on the inside and vinyl on the outside (both are high cost and tend to be higher build quality).
Wood. While they're not "maintenance-free", it costs just a few bucks every few years to reglaze them or repaint them. My house is 86, all original windows with leaded glass.

Vinyl if your looking cheap or renting, they have a life of around 10-15 years before they start to fail.

Fiberglass (ultrex) is like beefed up vinyl. Costs more but will last longer and preform better.

Wood for longevity but at a cost. They can last for hundreds of years with proper care and maintenance.

If you have the money though, go wood with aluminum clad exterior. Very expensive but has the benefits of wood with no exterior maintenance.

And finally we come to steel windows, fuck u'm!

Neither. If I needed new window frames I'd go for wood-aluminum frames. Aluminum on the outside gives you the ease of use and longevity of aluminum frames, wood on the inside gives you the insulation properties of wood with much lower maintenance requirements than full wood frames.
